In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of mechanisms of action of endocrine disrupting contaminants in fish, and the use of these mechanisms in the development and validation of predictive in vitro and in silico tools for the assessment of the endocrine disrupting potential of chemicals.
elucidating the mechanisms of action of chemicals that adversely impact endocrine function in fish.
understanding how chemicals can impact reproductive function through multiple mechanisms of action.

prochloraz is a potent inhibitor of aromatase in the fathead, but fenarimol is not.
prochloraz and to a lesser extent fenarimol can affect reproductive endocrine function of the fathead minnnow in a manner that is consistent with the effects of these chemicals in mammals.

the effects of proclhoraz on the fish were consistent with the effects of procholoraz on the mammalian hypothalamic pituiatry gonadal axis.

the two fungicides prochloraz andfenarimol, when tested at environmentally relevant concentrations, affected reproductive endocrine function through multiple mechanisms in the model fish species, fathead minnow.

the two fungicides tested have the potential to affect reproductive endocrine function through multiple mechanisms, including inhibition of steroidogenesis and antagonism of steroid receptors, and that these effects are not necessarily consistent across species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of multiple endpoints and assays, as well as multiple vertebrate models, will be necessary for a complete understanding of the mechanisms of action of these and similar chemicals.

the effects of chemicals on endocrine function are not limited to one or two specific modes of action, and that a more holistic assessment of endocrine function is necessary to understand the full spectrum of potential effects of a given chemical.
chemicals that have multiple modes of action, such as prochoraz and fenaraimol, may have different effects in different species.
